title: What Happens When You Get a Nosebleed?
sources: Cleveland Clinic, 'Nosebleed (Epistaxis)' ('The most common cause of nosebleeds is dry air'; dry environments include 'Heated indoor spaces'; 'Dry air causes your nasal membrane (the delicate tissue inside your nose) to dry out and become crusty or cracked', which makes it more likely to bleed when rubbed, picked or blown; the nose's many small blood vessels 'lie close to the inner surface of your nose'; the anterior nosebleed starts at the front of the nose: 'This is the most common type of epistaxis and usually isn't serious'; first aid: 'Sit up straight with your head slightly forward', breathe through your mouth, pinch the soft sides of your nose just above your nostrils; go to the ER if you can't stop it after more than 15 to 20 minutes of pinching; 'Have someone drive you to the nearest emergency room or call 911'): https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/13464-nosebleed-epistaxis

NHS, 'Nosebleed' ('Nosebleeds are not usually a sign of anything serious'; common causes: picking your nose, blowing your nose too hard, the inside of your nose being too dry; stop it: sit down and lean forward with your head tilted forward, pinch your nose just above your nostrils for 10 to 15 minutes, breathe through your mouth; go to A&E if the nosebleed lasts longer than 10 to 15 minutes; don't drive yourself): https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/nosebleed/

Tease (next video): Cleveland Clinic, 'Chills' ('Shivering causes your muscles to contract and relax, which warms up your body'; 'Many people feel chilled when they have a fever'): https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/21476-chills

lines.text: What happens when you get a nosebleed?
It looks scary, but the top cause? Plain old dry air.
